questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'South Asia: Geography and States' refers to.
questions.a: South Asia comprises eight states - India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Maldives and Afghanistan - with enormous demographic weight in India and varied political systems from stable democracies to military rules and monarchies.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'South Asia: Geography and States'.
questions.a: One region, many regimes: the subcontinent's states differ in size, systems and stability, which shapes every bilateral tie.

questions.q: Under which section is 'South Asia: Geography and States' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Military and Administration in Pakistan (source: leps103.txt South Asia definition, states and regime variety sections)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal's Politics' refers to.
questions.a: Pakistan alternated civilian and military rule with the army dominating security policy; Bangladesh born in 1971 through liberation war oscillated between civilian rule and military interventions; Nepal moved from monarchy to constitutional democracy through popular movements and a republican constitution.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal's Politics'.
questions.a: Each state's civil-military balance decides its democracy's depth, and 1971 redrew the region's map and politics.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal's Politics' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Conflict and Cooperation (source: leps103.txt Pakistan military rule, Bangladesh 1971 and Nepal democracy sections)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'India-Pakistan and Sri Lankan Conflicts' refers to.
questions.a: India-Pakistan conflict centres on Kashmir, wars of 1947-48, 1965 and 1971 and nuclearisation after the 1998 tests; India-Sri Lanka relations involve the Tamil question and Indian intervention, while China's rise shapes strategic calculations across the region.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'India-Pakistan and Sri Lankan Conflicts'.
questions.a: Nuclear tests of 1998 made the subcontinent's central conflict more dangerous and more stable at once - deterrence with brinkmanship.

questions.q: Under which section is 'India-Pakistan and Sri Lankan Conflicts' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: India and its Other Neighbours (source: leps103.txt Kashmir wars, 1998 tests and Sri Lanka sections)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Cooperation: SAARC and Regional Peace' refers to.
questions.a: South Asian cooperation runs through SAARC, founded in 1985 for collective self-reliance, and through trade and cultural exchanges; bilateral disputes, especially India-Pakistan, limit integration despite shared histories and democratisation trends across the region.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Cooperation: SAARC and Regional Peace'.
questions.a: SAARC shows both promise and paralysis: agreements exist, but the India-Pakistan freeze caps regional integration.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Cooperation: SAARC and Regional Peace' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Cooperation and Conflict: SAARC (source: leps103.txt SAARC founding, programmes and limits sections)
